captions: Hello, and welcome to Camday English, Stage 7. In this lesson: Every vote counts.
Recognise persuasive techniques in a speech.
Here are some new words. Rhetorical question. A question asked for effect, not for an answer. Statistic.
A fact shown as a number. Emotive. Making people feel strong emotions.
And some more words. Audience. The people who listen to or read something. Convince.
Make someone believe something. Slogan. A short, memorable phrase used in a campaign.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: a question asked for effect, not for an answer?
Now some grammar: Persuasive techniques. Persuasive writers use rhetorical questions, statistics,
emotive language, the rule of three and direct address (‘you’).
For example: Do we really want dirty streets? For example: 8 out of 10 students agree.
For example: Our school must be safe, clean and green.
Now listen, and read along. Vote for a greener school. Good morning, everyone.
My name is Lena, and I'm standing for the school council.
Did you know that our school throws away about forty bags of rubbish every week? Forty!
Most of it could be recycled. Do we really want our school to be part of the problem? Of course not.
We want a school that is cleaner, greener and smarter.
If you vote for me, I will start a recycling team in every year group.
I will ask the canteen to stop using plastic cutlery.
And I will plant a vegetable garden that every class can use.
Imagine walking past fresh tomatoes and sunflowers on your way to maths! Together, we can do this.
So on Friday, remember my slogan: ‘Think green – vote Lena!’
Another question. The video will stop. What is Lena standing for?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like rhetorical question, statistic, emotive.
You practised persuasive techniques. And you read Vote for a greener school. Now try the practice questions.
See you next time!

sections.title: You should, you must

q.prompt: Which word means “strongly ask someone to do something”?
q.reason: “urge” means strongly ask someone to do something.

options.fb: “benefit” means a good result or advantage.

captions: Hello, and welcome to Camday English, Stage 7. In this lesson: You should, you must.
Use modal verbs to make strong or polite suggestions in persuasive writing.
Here are some new words. Urge. Strongly ask someone to do something. Essential. Completely necessary.
Benefit. A good result or advantage.
And some more words. Volunteer. A person who works for free to help. Community.
The people living in one area. Commit. Promise to do something.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: strongly ask someone to do something?
Now some grammar: Modals for persuasion.
Use must, have to for strong necessity, should, ought to for advice, could, might for gentle suggestions.
For example: We must act now. For example: You should join the club. For example: You could help once a week.
Now listen, and read along. Join the Saturday Clean-Up. Join the Saturday Clean-up!
Our park belongs to all of us – so we all ought to look after it.
Every week, volunteers collect bottles, cans and plastic bags from the river banks.
Last month, they filled 63 bags in just one morning! You don't have to come every week.
You could join us for just one hour. Every pair of hands makes a difference.
Gloves and litter pickers are provided. You should wear old clothes and bring a drink.
The benefits are clear: a cleaner park, safer wildlife and a stronger community. We urge you to come along.
Our park needs you! Saturday, 9 to 11 a.m., meet at the park gates.
Another question. The video will stop. When is the clean-up?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like urge, essential, benefit. You practised modals for persuasion.
And you read Join the Saturday Clean-Up. Now try the practice questions. See you next time!
